subject: Polity
sub_topic: Effects of National Emergency on Fundamental Rights

concepts.name: Article 358: Suspension of Article 19 during National Emergency
key_dimensions: Automatic vs. discretionary suspension — Article 358 operates automatically upon proclamation, unlike Article 359 which requires a Presidential Order
Scope limitation: Only suspends Article 19 and only when Emergency is on grounds of 'war' or 'external aggression', NOT on grounds of 'armed rebellion'
Duration: Suspension lasts only for the duration of the Emergency, not indefinitely
44th Amendment restriction: Laws made and executive actions taken must be 'reasonably related' to the Emergency — State cannot use Emergency as cover for unrelated legislation

concepts.name: Article 359: Presidential Order Suspending Enforcement of Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Discretionary mechanism: President issues a separate Order specifying which Fundamental Rights (other than Articles 20 and 21) cannot be enforced
Judicial enforcement suspended, not the rights themselves — a critical distinction from Article 358 where the rights are actually suspended
Scope of suspension: Can apply to all or any of the Fundamental Rights under Part III (except Articles 20 and 21) and can be limited to specific territories
Parliament must approve the Order and it can be revoked by the President before Emergency ends; Parliament can also modify the Order

concepts.name: Articles 20 and 21: The Inviolable Core during National Emergency
key_dimensions: 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even during National Emergency — a direct response to the 1975–77 Emergency abuse
Pre-44th Amendment position: The original Constitution allowed suspension of Article 21 via Article 359, leading to the ADM Jabalpur controversy
Article 20 protections: Protection against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination — all remain fully operative during Emergency
UPSC trap: Distinguish between Article 358 (cannot touch Articles 20 & 21 at all) and Article 359 (President's Order expressly excludes Articles 20 & 21)

concepts.name: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976): The Habeas Corpus Case
key_dimensions: Supreme Court's majority ruling: During Emergency under Article 359, the right to move court for habeas corpus is suspended, effectively leaving detenues without remedy
Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent: Natural law argument — Right to life cannot be suspended even by a Presidential Order; considered one of the greatest judicial dissents in Indian history
Constitutional significance: Directly led to the 44th Amendment making Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable
Overruled by Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) judgment which affirmed that ADM Jabalpur was incorrectly decided

concepts.name: Distinction between Suspension of Rights (Article 358) vs. Suspension of Remedies (Article 359)
key_dimensions: Article 358: The Fundamental Right under Article 19 itself stands suspended — no violation can be claimed even after Emergency ends for actions taken during it
Article 359: The right remains on paper but the remedy (approaching courts) is suspended — once Emergency is revoked, the right is enforceable again and past violations can be questioned

Legislative competence implication: Under Article 358, Parliament/State can make laws inconsistent with Article 19; under Article 359, laws inconsistent with specified FRs are not void but unenforceable during Emergency
UPSC trap: Article 358 is self-executing; Article 359 requires a Presidential Order to be effective

concepts.name: Effect of National Emergency on State List — Legislative Powers of Parliament
key_dimensions: Article 250: Parliament acquires power to legislate on State List subjects during National Emergency — this is an expansion of legislative competence, not a transfer
Laws made by Parliament under Article 250 cease to have effect six months after Emergency ends (not immediately)
State legislatures are NOT suspended — they can still legislate on State List subjects, creating potential conflict resolved by Parliamentary law prevailing
Linkage to Fundamental Rights: Parliament using expanded powers may enact laws restricting FRs of citizens in states, compounding the Emergency's impact

concepts.name: Effect of National Emergency on Financial Relations between Centre and States
key_dimensions: Article 354: President can modify provisions relating to distribution of revenues between Centre and States during National Emergency
This modification must be approved by Parliament and ceases after the financial year in which Emergency ends
Distinction from President's Rule (Article 356): Financial provisions are altered differently — Article 354 applies only during National Emergency, not State Emergency
UPSC trap: The modification is not automatic — it requires a Presidential Order under Article 354, unlike some other Emergency effects

concepts.name: Extension of Tenure of Lok Sabha and State Legislatures during National Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 83(2): Parliament can by law extend the tenure of Lok Sabha beyond 5 years, one year at a time, during National Emergency
Article 172: Similarly, tenure of State Legislative Assemblies can be extended by Parliament (not state legislature) during National Emergency
Critical condition: Extension ceases automatically within six months after Emergency ends — Parliament cannot make the extension permanent
UPSC trap: It is Parliament (not the President) that extends the tenure, and it applies to State Assemblies too — a significant centralizing effect

concepts.name: Judicial Review of National Emergency Proclamation
key_dimensions: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): Courts can examine whether the proclamation was mala fide or based on wholly extraneous grounds
44th Amendment introduced Article 352(5): Presidential satisfaction must be on the basis of written communication by Union Cabinet, making it justiciable to some extent
S.R. Bommai principle (though directly about Article 356) extended to suggest floor tests and objective criteria matter — influences Emergency jurisprudence
Limitation: Courts apply a very deferential standard of review for national security matters; they examine procedure and mala fides, not the merits of the threat assessment

concepts.name: 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978): Safeguards against Emergency Abuse
key_dimensions: Changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' as a ground for Emergency — raising the threshold significantly
Made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable during Emergency under Article 359
Required written recommendation of the Union Cabinet (not just PM) before President can proclaim Emergency — prevents unilateral action by PM

Introduced special majority for revocation in Lok Sabha: Emergency can be revoked by a simple majority of total membership of Lok Sabha on a special sitting demanded by 1/10th of members — a new check absent before 1978

concepts.name: Role of Parliament in Approval and Continuation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 352(4): Emergency must be approved by both Houses of Parliament by special majority (2/3 of members present and voting + majority of total membership) within one month of proclamation
UPSC trap: If Lok Sabha is dissolved and Emergency is proclaimed, it must be approved by Rajya Sabha within one month AND Lok Sabha must approve within 30 days of its reconstitution
Continuation requires renewal by Parliament every six months with the same special majority
Revocation mechanism: President can revoke on his own, OR must revoke if Lok Sabha passes a resolution by simple majority at a special sitting (demanded by 1/10th of total LS members)

concepts.name: Impact on Rights of Arrested Persons: Articles 22 and 32 during Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 22 (Protection against arbitrary arrest) can be suspended by Presidential Order under Article 359 — enabling preventive detention without the usual constitutional safeguards
Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) can also be suspended under Article 359 — the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to enforce FRs can be taken away
High Court jurisdiction under Article 226 is NOT suspended during Emergency — a crucial distinction; HCs can still issue writs for enforcement of non-suspended rights
UPSC trap: Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359 but Article 226 cannot be — making HCs potentially the last refuge during Emergency

concepts.name: Grounds for Proclamation of National Emergency: War, External Aggression, Armed Rebellion
key_dimensions: Three grounds under Article 352(1): War, External Aggression, and Armed Rebellion (substituted for 'internal disturbance' by 44th Amendment)
Preventive Emergency: Can be proclaimed even before actual occurrence of war/external aggression if threat is imminent — 'the security of India or a part thereof is threatened'

Armed Rebellion ground (internal): Linkage to Article 358 is critical — Article 358 (suspension of Article 19) does NOT apply when Emergency is on grounds of armed rebellion, only for war/external aggression
Historical instances: 1962 (Chinese aggression), 1971 (Pakistani aggression), 1975 (internal disturbance — the most controversial) — UPSC tests knowledge of grounds used

concepts.name: Coexistence of Multiple Emergencies and Their Compounding Effect on Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Constitutional provisions allow simultaneous operation of National Emergency (Article 352), State Emergency (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360)
During simultaneous National and State Emergency: Parliament legislates for both Union and State lists; executive control passes to Centre — complete centralization
Effect on FRs compounds: National Emergency suspends/restricts FRs via Articles 358/359 while State Emergency removes democratic accountability in states
Financial Emergency (Article 360) does NOT suspend any Fundamental Rights — a critical UPSC distinction; it only affects financial provisions and salaries of government servants

concepts.name: Financial Emergency (Article 360) vs. National Emergency: Impact on Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Financial Emergency does NOT affect Fundamental Rights at all — no provision akin to Articles 358 or 359 exists for Article 360
President can give directions to states to observe financial propriety and reduce salaries of government servants including judges — but this is not a FR restriction
Proclamation requires simple majority in Parliament (unlike special majority for National Emergency) and remains in force till revoked — no periodic renewal needed
UPSC trap: Students confuse Financial Emergency with National Emergency; only the latter affects Fundamental Rights and requires special majority for continuation

concepts.name: Preventive Detention Laws during National Emergency: MISA and Constitutional Validity
key_dimensions: Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 was extensively used during the 1975 Emergency to detain political opponents without trial
Constitutional basis: Article 22(3) to (7) allows Parliament to make preventive detention laws; Article 359 Orders further suspended the right to challenge such detention
39th Amendment (1975) placed MISA in the Ninth Schedule to immunize it from judicial review — later struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)
Post-44th Amendment safeguard: Even under MISA-type laws, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended, providing minimum protection against custodial torture and ex post facto punishment

concepts.name: Press Freedom and Article 19(1)(a) during National Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 19(1)(a) — freedom of speech and expression (including press freedom) — is suspended under Article 358 during Emergency on grounds of war/external aggression
1975 Emergency: Pre-censorship of press was imposed; newspapers left editorial columns blank in protest — a landmark episode in Indian press history
Distinction: During Emergency on armed rebellion grounds, Article 358 does not apply, so Article 19(1)(a) is NOT automatically suspended (only through a specific Article 359 Order)
Post-Emergency, laws enacted during Emergency that restrict Article 19 rights become void six months after Emergency ends unless specifically re-enacted by Parliament

concepts.name: Right to Equality (Articles 14 and 15) during National Emergency
key_dimensions: Articles 14 and 15 are NOT covered by Article 358 (which only covers Article 19) — they remain enforceable unless specifically included in a Presidential Order under Article 359

UPSC trap: Students assume all Fundamental Rights are suspended during National Emergency — only Article 19 is automatically suspended (Article 358); others require a specific Presidential Order under Article 359
Historical abuse: During 1975 Emergency, while formal suspension of Article 14 was not ordered, selective enforcement and executive highhandedness effectively undermined equality
Judicial response: Courts retained jurisdiction to enforce Article 14 during Emergency (as no Order excluded it in 1975–77), though in practice they exercised extreme restraint

concepts.name: Evolution of Supreme Court's Attitude toward Emergency Powers: From ADM Jabalpur to Puttaswamy
key_dimensions: ADM Jabalpur (1976): Court's capitulation — majority held that during Emergency, no person has locus standi to challenge detention; life and liberty can be suspended
Minerva Mills (1980): Court reasserted basic structure doctrine; held that Fundamental Rights are part of basic structure and cannot be permanently abrogated even by Emergency
Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017): Nine-judge bench unanimously declared ADM Jabalpur was incorrectly decided; Right to Life and Personal Liberty is inherent and cannot be taken away
Significance for UPSC: This evolution shows that constitutional morality has strengthened post-Emergency; Puttaswamy is the current legal position overriding ADM Jabalpur

concepts.name: Special Provisions for North-Eastern States and Scheduled Areas during Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 371 series: Special provisions for NE states (Nagaland, Mizoram, etc.) coexist with Emergency provisions — Emergency does not automatically override these special protections
Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas: Tribal rights and customary law protections under these schedules are not automatically suspended during National Emergency

UPSC angle: Interaction between Emergency powers and special category provisions is a less-tested but important area — Emergency proclamation applies uniformly but special provisions may limit executive action
Armed Forces Special Powers Act (AFSPA): Operates in 'disturbed areas' independent of Emergency proclamation — distinction between AFSPA regime and Emergency regime on FRs is frequently confused
